html:
One of the first and most important Roman roads, begun in 312 BCE by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus. It ran south from Rome to Capua, and was later extended to Beneventum, Tarentum and Brundisium (Brindisi), the port for Greece and the East.

The Roman Republic built it to move armies during the Samnite Wars for control of southern Italy. It ran straight where it could, on a bed of layered stone with a paved top, drains and milestones. Romans called it the "queen of roads".

It set the pattern for a network that grew to tens of thousands of kilometres, from the Via Flaminia going north to the Via Egnatia across the Balkans. Tombs lined it outside Rome. In 71 BCE, after Spartacus' revolt, some 6,000 captured slaves were crucified along it between Capua and Rome. Long stretches can still be walked today. Other empires built road networks too, like the Inca roads.
